For each encoded instance length $n$ and explicitly declared public data $p$, a **quantum query algorithm** is a specified finite circuit protocol on its query and work registers, fixed independently of the hidden instance $z$ at fixed $(n,p)$. The hidden encoding labels the oracle instance; it is not supplied as a readable input register. A register is a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with its ordered computational basis; an $r$-qubit register uses the lexicographic bit-string basis, with the first wire most significant ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). The finite promise-computation model [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]] supplies the public-classical-input, zero-initialized ancillary-register, ordered-output-tuple, and final-predicate conventions. Its classical input and terminal predicate receive only the declared public data, not the hidden encoding. Circuit syntax fixes the ordered wires and finite gate list [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], and its denotation fixes the chronological gate composition [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. The execution tree starts in the standard public-input basis state with all other registers zero. Any explicit preparation interface is executed as a specified finite prefix of unitary or instrument nodes of this tree, with its preparation calls and other resource costs charged under the declared access contract. Intermediate measurements and classical feed-forward are represented by finite trees of instrument outcomes and branch-specific unitary operations. In the ordinary oracle-only model, all preparation operations, nonoracle gates and instruments, branch-control rules, and terminal output rules are independent of the hidden instance at fixed $(n,p)$; later operations may depend on observed outcomes. For each instantiated oracle, [[def-qa-finite-branch-output-law]] gives the normalized output law of this tree with its public classical input. The output is interpreted according to the decision bit or search relation in [[def-qa-task-and-promise-domain]].

In the ordinary oracle-only model, hidden-instance dependence enters only through the designated oracle calls. Explicit public parameters and arithmetic inputs remain available when the task declares them. Any additional instance-dependent state preparation or data-access operation is a separately declared and charged resource. Oracle-only lower bounds compare instances with the same public data and without such additional input access; the hidden encoding itself supplies none.

A **$T$-query algorithm** has at most $T$ designated calls to the oracle $U_{f_z}$ of [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]] and [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]] on every execution branch for every promised $z\in P_n$. Calls count once each; gates in the circuit outside those designated calls are not query calls. Uniformity is asserted only when the family satisfies [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. A controlled call has the block action in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and is available only when the access contract explicitly supplies and charges it. An inverse call to this XOR oracle has the same action as an ordinary call by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]; inverses of other unitaries use the separate availability and charge convention in [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]].

Fix an encoded input $x$ and a finite rooted execution tree on the same declared finite register $H_n$ at every node. Its root state is the density operator of the standard input basis state with zero-initialized work registers. Every nonterminal node is either a unitary endomorphism $U:H_n\to H_n$ or a finite instrument $(\mathcal I_a)_{a\in\Omega_h}$ whose branch maps are from $\mathcal L(H_n)$ to $\mathcal L(H_n)$. The observed outcome label $a$ is retained for classical feed-forward, while a hidden Kraus label is not a branch. The tree has finite depth and finite outcome sets.

Assign the root weight $w(\varnothing)=1$. At a unitary edge set $\rho_{h'}=U\rho_hU^\dagger$ and $w(h')=w(h)$. At an instrument node set $q_{h,a}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_a(\rho_h))$ and $w(ha)=w(h)q_{h,a}$. If $q_{h,a}>0$, set $\rho_{ha}=\mathcal I_a(\rho_h)/q_{h,a}$; if $q_{h,a}=0$, that child and its descendants have weight zero and contribute no state or output weight. The instrument and conditional-state conventions are those of [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]].

At each positive-weight leaf $\ell$, the ordered output wires have a fixed length $m$ and are disjoint from the remaining wires $W_\ell$. For $z\in\{0,1\}^m$ and a bit string $v$ on $W_\ell$, let $e_{\ell,z,v}$ be the full-register computational-basis vector with those bits in their declared wire positions. Define the leaf output weight and total output law by
$$q_\ell(z):=\sum_{v\in\{0,1\}^{|W_\ell|}}\langle \rho_\ell e_{\ell,z,v},e_{\ell,z,v}\rangle_{\rm root},\qquad P(z\mid x):=\sum_{\ell\text{ positive-weight leaf}}w(\ell)q_\ell(z).$$
The classical output predicate $A_n(x,z)$ selects the acceptance event by summing $P(z\mid x)$ over the finite set of accepted strings. This definition extends the terminal-output convention of [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]] to finite instrument branches; the verification proves that $P(\cdot\mid x)$ is a normalized probability law and every acceptance probability lies in $[0,1]$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, fix an ordered
orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following are
equivalent: $\Phi$ is completely positive; $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is
non-negative; and $\Phi$ has a finite Kraus representation.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]),
with the root convention that
each inner product is linear in its first argument. Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for
the complex-linear endomorphisms of $H$ and $\mathcal L(H,K)$ for the
complex-linear maps from $H$ to $K$ ([[def-linear-map]]). A **finite Kraus
representation** of a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ is a finite family
$(K_a)_{a\in A}\subseteq\mathcal L(H,K)$ such that

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $a,b\ge 0$ and let $f:\{0,1\}^{a}\to\{0,1\}^{b}$ be a total function. The **standard bit-flip query** for $f$ is the coherent XOR action
$$
U_f|x\rangle|y\rangle=|x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle
$$
on the ordered $a$-bit address register followed by the ordered $b$-bit target register. Here $\oplus$ is componentwise addition modulo two, and words label the ordered computational basis as in [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] and [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. The address is unchanged. One invocation is one query under [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]; its query cost is separate from elementary gate cost.

The map is an involution and is unitary by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. No injectivity of $f$ is assumed.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

All bits are in $\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}$, with addition denoted by $\oplus$ and multiplication by juxtaposition. On three distinct ordered computational-basis wires, define the Toffoli gate $T$ and Fredkin gate $F$ by
$$
T|a,b,t\rangle=|a,b,t\oplus ab\rangle,
$$
and
$$
F|0,a,b\rangle=|0,a,b\rangle,\qquad F|1,a,b\rangle=|1,b,a\rangle.
$$
These basis actions extend linearly. Wire order is exactly the order displayed; the first two wires of $T$ are controls and the third is its target, while the first wire of $F$ is its control and the other two are conditionally swapped. Negative-control variants mean conjugating the chosen positive control by $X$ before and after the gate. These are fixed arity-three labels in the declared finite gate alphabet, not implicit access to arbitrary multicontrol gates. Their reversibility is established in [[lem-qc-x-cnot-toffoli-and-fredkin-are-involutions]].

derivations.claim: At an instrument node with outcome maps $(\mathcal I_a)_{a\in\Omega}$, choose a finite Kraus family $(K_{a,r})_r$ for each $\mathcal I_a$ by [F3]–[F4]. The formula in [F5] shows that their union is a Kraus family for the total map $\Phi=\sum_a\mathcal I_a$. The trace identity in [F3] makes $\Phi$ trace-preserving, so [F6] gives $\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}^\dagger K_{a,r}=I$.

Label every node of the finite execution tree by the number of oracle calls already made on its path. For each $t<T$, order the finitely many nonoracle nodes in that query-count slice by tree depth, execute each node on histories with its observed-outcome prefix, and use the identity on histories already at their next query or terminal node. This places every next query at one common slot while preserving each branch's transitions; histories that have terminated are inactive in this and every later slot. The retained outcome history identifies the branches that still make a query. On every inactive branch, conditionally swap the caller's entire $N$-level address register with a fresh register of the same dimension initialized to $|0\rangle$, and swap the caller's response qubit with a fresh qubit initialized to $|+\rangle$, prepared using $H$ from [F11]. The address-register swap is the finite basis permutation exchanging the two ordered register factors; controlling it on the retained history gives a finite input-independent unitary. After the ordinary oracle call, reverse both conditional swaps. On an inactive branch the oracle acts on $|0\rangle|+\rangle$ as either $I$ or $X$ on the response, both of which fix $|+\rangle$; the caller's address and response, including any entanglement with work, are restored. Active branches are unchanged, so this pads the slot without controlled oracle access.

Add a finite label register $L$ with orthonormal basis $|a,r\rangle_L$ and use the same factor order throughout, defining $V:H\to L\otimes H$ by $V\psi=\sum_{a,r}|a,r\rangle_L\otimes K_{a,r}\psi$. Orthonormality [F9], the adjoint identity [F7], and step 1.1 give $\langle V\psi,V\phi\rangle=\sum_{a,r}\langle K_{a,r}\psi,K_{a,r}\phi\rangle=\langle\psi,\phi\rangle$; hence $V$ is an isometry. For any density operator $\rho$, projecting the label onto the outcome subspace spanned by $\{|a,r\rangle_L:r\}$ and discarding the label leaves $\sum_rK_{a,r}\rho K_{a,r}^\dagger$; orthogonality removes all unequal-label cross terms. By [F5] this is exactly $\mathcal I_a(\rho)$.

In the common codomain $L\otimes H$, let $J\psi=|0\rangle_L\otimes\psi$ be the clean-ancilla embedding. The images under $J$ and $V$ of one orthonormal basis of $H$ are orthonormal lists of the same finite length in this same finite-dimensional space. Choose a finite spanning basis by [F10]; process it in order, subtracting its projections onto the current list and appending the normalized nonzero remainder. This finite Gram–Schmidt procedure completes each list to an orthonormal basis. Mapping the first completed basis to the second defines a unitary $U$ with $UJ=V$, so the instrument node is realized by an ordinary unitary and retained outcome/Kraus labels.

Keep each observed outcome in an orthogonal record register; hidden Kraus labels remain orthogonal environment labels and are not used by later controls. Induct over the finite execution tree, comparing the unnormalized system density for each observed history after tracing out its hidden labels. A unitary node applies the same branch unitary on every hidden-label subspace, and an instrument node has child reduced density $\mathcal I_a(\rho)$ by step 2.1, so each history's unnormalized system density agrees with the original instrument computation. At terminal histories, measuring the declared output and ignoring the orthogonal records therefore gives exactly the output law in [F2].

Insert one such ordinary call in each of the $T$ slots, using input-independent history controls for active and padded branches. Steps 1.1–4.1 preserve every output probability, and step 1.2 pads only branches with fewer than $T$ calls. Thus the resulting pure-state circuit has exactly $T$ ordinary XOR calls and the original output distribution.

$$O_x|j,b,w\rangle=|j,b\oplus x_{j+1},w\rangle,\qquad 0\le j<N.$$
The response register is one qubit and the work register is any declared finite tensor product. For $N=2^n$, this is the standard bit query of [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]] under the big-endian address encoding; for general $N$, it is the same XOR basis action on the $N$-level address register.

A $T$-query algorithm is a finite circuit whose only input-dependent operations are at most $T$ invocations of $O_x$ on every execution branch. By [[lem-qa-14-coherent-query-normal-form]], it may be analyzed as a pure initial unit vector, input-independent unitaries between exactly $T$ ordinary queries, and one final measurement. The query coordinate counts these oracle invocations under [[def-qa-quantum-query-complexity]]; response preparation, verification queries, gates, and classical work are stated separately. For a decision task, bounded error means the correct answer has probability at least $2/3$ on every promised input, as in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]]. For a finding task, the same threshold applies to producing a valid witness on each promised input. linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.

[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $I_H:H\to H$ denote the identity map $x\mapsto x$. An **effect** on $H$ is an endomorphism $E$ such that both $E$ and $I_H-E$ are non-negative in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. A **finite complete positive family** is a nonempty finite list $(E_1,\ldots,E_n)$ of non-negative endomorphisms with $\sum_{a=1}^n E_a=I_H$. The next lemma proves that every member of such a family is an effect, so the family is a finite complete effect family. This is algebraic data only; it does not assert a measurement law.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

A quantum or classical solver in [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] and [[def-qa-classical-query-algorithm]] for a decision task $(Y,N)$ of [[def-qa-task-and-promise-domain]] has **bounded error** (with the QA convention) if its normalized output law assigns probability at least $2/3$ to the correct answer for every encoded promised instance. A search solver has bounded error if, for every encoded $z$ in its domain $D$, its output law assigns probability at least $2/3$ to outputs $w$ satisfying $(z,w)\in R$. The guarantee is worst-case per instance, not averaged over an input distribution. The constant $2/3$ is a convention; amplification and its query/access cost are separate results.

For quantum algorithms the success event is evaluated from the normalized finite-branch output law of [[def-qa-finite-branch-output-law]]. Its normalization follows from the finite instrument and unitary branches in that definition; the success threshold remains a per-instance condition.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_j)$ for $E$. Positivity of $E$ and $I-E$ puts each eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ in $[0,1]$. Put $\delta=\psi-\phi$. The acceptance-probability difference equals $\langle E\delta,\psi\rangle+\langle E\phi,\delta\rangle$. By [F2], unit normalization, and step 1.1, its absolute value is at most $\|E\delta\|\|\psi\|+\|E\phi\|\|\delta\|\le2\|\delta\|$. The probability gap in [F3] is at least $1/3$, so $\|\psi-\phi\|\ge1/6$.

**Input:** An integer $N\ge1$, a power of two $M=2^m$ with $N\le M<2N$, a padded address register $A_M$ with basis $|j\rangle$ for $0\le j<M$, a response bit, and the raw XOR oracle $O_x$ whose address input is the $N$-level register with basis $|q\rangle$ for $0\le q<N$. If $N=M$, identify $A_M$ with the raw address register. If $N<M$, supply a separate clean $N$-level raw-address register $Q_N$ initialized to $|0\rangle$, together with clean comparator and routing workspace.

**Output:** The zero-completed query action $|j,b\rangle\mapsto|j,b\oplus\widetilde x_j\rangle$ on $A_M$ and the response bit, where $\widetilde x_j=x_{j+1}$ for $j<N$ and $\widetilde x_j=0$ for $j\ge N$, with every added register restored to its specified computational-basis zero state.

**Instructions:**

2. Compute the validity bit $v=[j<N]$ into a clean bit by a reversible binary comparison. For most-significant-first address bits $j_r$ and the fixed binary digits $N_r$, initialize $E_0=1,L_0=0$ and update

**Input:** An integer $N\ge1$, standard Boolean XOR-query access $O_x|q,b,w\rangle=|q,b\oplus x_{q+1},w\rangle$ on the ordered $N$-level address register of [[def-qa-14-boolean-search-query-model]], with $x\in P_N$ from [[def-qa-14-search-promise]], and no information about whether $x=0^N$ or $x=e_i$. Any auxiliary registers used by the procedure start in their declared clean states; the procedure returns all subroutine workspace clean before reuse or termination.

**Gate model:** Inherit the nonoracle model of [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]]: exact $H$ and $X$ are callable, with each occurrence charged as one elementary gate, including the $m$ Hadamards preparing the uniform address state and all response preparations. The exact reflection $R_s$ on the $M$ padded addresses is supplied either as an explicitly costed primitive or by a declared costed exact circuit over the selected alphabet. All preparation and reflection costs are counted separately from raw oracle queries.

**Output:** The symbol no and no candidate if verification fails; otherwise yes and a verified marked coordinate.

**Instructions:**

1. Set $m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil$, $M=2^m$, so $N\le M<2N$, and hard-code the schedule parameter $t_0=1$. This is a fixed schedule; it is not an assertion that the actual input has one mark.
2. Set $K=\lceil\sqrt M\rceil$ and $q=1-2/M$. Compute exactly $T_0(q)=1$, $T_1(q)=q$, and $T_{r+1}(q)=2qT_r(q)-T_{r-1}(q)$ for $1\le r<2K+1$. For $k=0,\ldots,K$, compute $p_k=(1-T_{2k+1}(q))/2$ and choose the least $k$ maximizing this finite list.
3. Prepare the uniform state on $M$ addresses and apply the Grover iterate of [[alg-qa-11-grover-iterate]] exactly $k$ times, implementing each padded bit query by [[alg-qa-14-zero-completion-query-simulation]]. Allocate the clean raw-address, comparison, and routing workspace required by each call; return it clean before the next call. The iterate's phase-kickback response is supplied in $| - \rangle$ as specified by that iterate.
4. Measure the padded address $j$. Prepare a fresh response bit in $|0\rangle$ and use [[alg-qa-14-zero-completion-query-simulation]] for the candidate-verification query, with its required clean workspace. Measure the response bit. If $j<N$ and this bit is $1$, output yes and original coordinate $j+1$. Otherwise output no and no candidate. Return all clean workspace to zero.

The schedule is defined on every input in $P_N$ and never receives an actual marked count. The recurrence and gate costs are classical/nonoracle costs; every simulated Grover or verification query uses one standard raw bit query.

For $N\ge1$ and $M=2^m$ with $N\le M<2N$, the procedure of [[alg-qa-14-zero-completion-query-simulation]] implements exactly one zero-completed XOR query per raw $N$-address query, restores all scratch registers, and uses no controlled oracle call.

Let $N=2^n$, let $1\le t\le N$, put $q=1-2t/N$ and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt{t/N}$. If $T_0(q)=1$, $T_1(q)=q$, and $T_{r+1}(q)=2qT_r(q)-T_{r-1}(q)$, then for every integer $k\ge0$,
$$(1-T_{2k+1}(q))/2=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).$$
Thus the exact rational values used by the known-count Grover schedule equal its actual marked-address probabilities.

Put $a=t/N$ and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a$. If $0<a\le1/2$, some integer $k$ with $0\le k\le K=\lceil1/\sqrt a\rceil$ has
$$p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\ge1-a.$$
If $1/2<a\le1$, $k=0$ lies in this range and $p_0=a>1/2$. The real-valued optimizer $k_*=\pi/(4\theta)-1/2$ is not in general an integer.

For every integer $N\ge1$, use the identity encoding of [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] and let $P_N=\{0^N\}\cup\{e_i:1\le i\le N\}$, where $0^N$ is the all-zero string and $e_i$ has a $1$ exactly in coordinate $i$. This is a promise decision task in the sense of [[def-qa-task-and-promise-domain]]: its yes set is $\{e_i:1\le i\le N\}$, its no set is $\{0^N\}$, and its output is $\operatorname{OR}(x)$.

For the associated search task, set $\ell_N=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil$ and let $\operatorname{bin}_{\ell_N}(k)$ be the length-$\ell_N$ binary expansion of $k$, most significant bit first and padded with leading zeros. Its promise domain is $P_N$ and its witness relation is
$$R_N=\{(0^N,\operatorname{bin}_{\ell_N}(0))\}\cup\{(e_i,\operatorname{bin}_{\ell_N}(i)):1\le i\le N\}.$$
The output labels none and $i$ mean these encoded strings for $0$ and $i$, respectively. The marked query address corresponding to $e_i$ is $j=i-1$ in [[def-qa-14-boolean-search-query-model]]. Verifying a measured candidate costs a separate query. No correctness condition is imposed outside $P_N$.

The maximizing choice in [F1] has value at least $p_0$, and [F3] identifies every list value with a probability at most $1$, so the selected success probability is $1$. citations.quote: For the promise $P_N=\{0^N,e_1,\ldots,e_N\}$ of [[def-qa-14-search-promise]], every bounded-error quantum algorithm deciding whether the input is zero or one-marked uses at least $\sqrt N/24$ standard bit queries. Every bounded-error finder that outputs a marked coordinate on each $e_i$ and none on $0^N$ also uses at least $\sqrt N/24$ standard bit queries. The decision part satisfies the stronger bound $T\ge\sqrt N/12$.

On every promised input of [[def-qa-14-search-promise]], the fixed-one procedure [[alg-qa-14-one-marked-search-with-verification]] returns the correct decision and, on a one-marked input, its marked coordinate with probability at least $1-1/M$, where $M=2^{\lceil\log_2N\rceil}$ and $M=1$ when $N=1$. In particular, its one-marked success probability is at least $1-1/N$; when $N=1$ it succeeds with certainty. On $0^N$ verification always returns no.

For every $N\ge1$, [[alg-qa-14-one-marked-search-with-verification]] uses at most $3\sqrt{2N}$ standard bit queries, including the final candidate verification. Hence its query cost is $O(\sqrt N)$. Address comparison, reversible computation, recurrence evaluation, state preparation, reflection gates, and all other nonoracle work are separate costs; no polynomial-time claim is made.

For every integer $N\ge1$, use the identity encoding of [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] and let $P_N=\{0^N\}\cup\{e_i:1\le i\le N\}$, where $0^N$ is the all-zero string and $e_i$ has a $1$ exactly in coordinate $i$. This is a promise decision task in the sense of [[def-qa-task-and-promise-domain]]: its yes set is $\{e_i:1\le i\le N\}$, its no set is $\{0^N\}$, and its output is $\operatorname{OR}(x)$.

For the associated search task, set $\ell_N=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil$ and let $\operatorname{bin}_{\ell_N}(k)$ be the length-$\ell_N$ binary expansion of $k$, most significant bit first and padded with leading zeros. Its promise domain is $P_N$ and its witness relation is
$$R_N=\{(0^N,\operatorname{bin}_{\ell_N}(0))\}\cup\{(e_i,\operatorname{bin}_{\ell_N}(i)):1\le i\le N\}.$$
The output labels none and $i$ mean these encoded strings for $0$ and $i$, respectively. The marked query address corresponding to $e_i$ is $j=i-1$ in [[def-qa-14-boolean-search-query-model]]. Verifying a measured candidate costs a separate query. No correctness condition is imposed outside $P_N$.

For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. For nonempty $P_n$, a finite circuit and finite branch sets ensure that this maximum exists; a solver whose branch counts are not uniformly bounded has infinite worst-case query cost. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

In the pure query model, ordinary gates outside the oracle calls are uncharged by the query coordinate. If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. Bounded-error query cost uses the same worst-case maximum; its success threshold is the per-instance condition in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]], not an average over oracle inputs.

For $N\ge3$, the one-run success probability in [F2] is at least $1-1/N\ge2/3$. For $N=1$, [F2] gives certainty. Each run has success probability at least $1/2$ by [F2]; conditional independence of the fresh runs gives failure probability at most $(1-1/2)^2=1/4$, hence success at least $3/4$.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For the address register of [[def-qa-14-boolean-search-query-model]], let $\Pi_j$ be the orthogonal projection onto address $j$, tensored with the identity on the response and work registers, for $0\le j<N$. For any finite input domain $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^N$, define the mismatch matrix $\Delta_j$ by $(\Delta_j)_{x,y}=1$ when $x_{j+1}\ne y_{j+1}$ and $0$ otherwise, for $x,y\in D$. This model has no separate skip-query address; if an implementation adjoins one, its basis projection is included as an additional orthogonal summand.

For a $T$-query algorithm in the model of [[def-qa-14-boolean-search-query-model]], let $\psi_t^0$ be its unit state on input $0^N$ immediately before query $t+1$, for $0\le t<T$, and set $q_{t,i}=\|\Pi_{i-1}\psi_t^0\|^2$. If $\psi_T^0$ and $\psi_T^i$ are the final unit states on $0^N$ and $e_i$, then
$$\|\psi_T^i-\psi_T^0\|\le2\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sqrt{q_{t,i}}.$$

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

derivations.claim: Let $|s\rangle=\frac12(|0\rangle+|1\rangle+|2\rangle+|3\rangle)$ be the first query's address state, with any fixed unit response and work state. By [F1], $\|s\|=1$ and each address probability is $q_{0,i}=1/4$. Hence $\sum_iq_{0,i}=1$.

Put $e_3=|3\rangle$ and $u=s-e_3$. By [F1], $\langle s,e_3\rangle_{\rm root}=1/2$, so $\|u\|^2=1+1-2(1/2)=1$. The map $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ is an orthogonal projection by [F5], and $R=I-2P_u$ satisfies $R^*R=R^2=I$. By [F2], $P_us=\langle s,u\rangle_{\rm root}u=(1/2)u$, so $Rs=s-u=e_3$. Use this input-independent reflection between the first and second queries. The all-zero oracle is identity, so the second pre-query address state is $|3\rangle$; thus $q_{1,4}=1$, $q_{1,1}=q_{1,2}=q_{1,3}=0$, and $\sum_iq_{1,i}=1$.

Therefore the sum of squared bounds is at most $3\cdot1^2+3^2=12$, and the average squared distance is at most $12/4=3$. Fix an integer $n\ge0$, put $N=2^n$, and let $D_n=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. The big-endian encoding $\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to D_n$ is a bijection by [[thm-qc-bitstring-index-is-bijection]], so identify each address word $w$ with its slot $x=\operatorname{enc}_n(w)$. A search instance is a total Boolean function $f:D_n\to\{0,1\}$, equivalently the word-indexed function $w\mapsto f(\operatorname{enc}_n(w))$. Its marked set is $M=\{x\in D_n:f(x)=1\}$ and its marked count is $t=|M|$. The standard bit query is the coherent XOR action $U_f|x,b\rangle=|x,b\oplus f(x)\rangle$; the associated phase query is $O_M|x\rangle=(-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle$. One standard bit query implements this phase action with a response qubit prepared in $|-\rangle$, by [[thm-qa-bit-query-to-phase-query]]. A measured candidate $x$ is verified by a separate standard bit query. Knowing $t$ is additional classical input; no count promise is made in the unknown-count version. A correct search output is a verified $x\in M$. The distinguished output none is used only by a procedure whose input includes the exact fact $t=0$; it is not a finite-time test for emptiness when $t$ is unknown.

The number $n$ may be zero, so $N=1$ and the address register then has its one-dimensional empty-word basis. The phase query is uncontrolled; no controlled-query capability is part of this definition.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

For unit vectors $u,v$ in a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, let $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ and $P_v=|v\rangle\langle v|$. Then
$$D(P_u,P_v)=\sqrt{1-|\langle u|v\rangle_D|^2},$$
where $\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle_D$ is the Dirac pairing converted from the root library's first-argument-linear inner product.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$X:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ be self-adjoint. There are non-negative
endomorphisms $X_+,X_-$ such that

$$X=X_+-X_-,\qquad \langle X_+u,X_-v\rangle=0\quad(u,v\in\mathcal H),$$

and

$$\|X\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(X_+)+\operatorname{tr}(X_-).$$

If $\operatorname{tr}(X)=0$, then
$\|X\|_1=2\operatorname{tr}(X_+)=2\operatorname{tr}(X_-)$. 

The trace norm is the finite singular-value norm from
[[def-qc-trace-norm]].

Let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $\{E_a\}_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be any finite POVM. If $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$ and $q_a=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_a)$, then
$$\frac12\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|p_a-q_a|\le D(\rho,\sigma).$$
The two-effect projective measurement from the Holevo–Helstrom theorem attains equality.

For the promise $P_N=\{0^N,e_1,\ldots,e_N\}$ of [[def-qa-14-search-promise]], every bounded-error quantum algorithm deciding whether the input is zero or one-marked uses at least $\sqrt N/24$ standard bit queries. Every bounded-error finder that outputs a marked coordinate on each $e_i$ and none on $0^N$ also uses at least $\sqrt N/24$ standard bit queries. The decision part satisfies the stronger bound $T\ge\sqrt N/12$.

derivations.claim: Let $|s\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|j\rangle$, $P_s=|s\rangle\langle s|$, and let the fixed marked coordinate be $i$. Its query address is $i-1$, so the phase query $O_i=I-2|i-1\rangle\langle i-1|$ sends $s$ to the unit vector $\psi_i=s-2|i-1\rangle/\sqrt N$ because it only flips one basis sign; set $P_{\psi_i}=|\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|$. Orthonormality [F2] gives $\langle s,\psi_i\rangle_D=1-2/N$; [F5]–[F6] give $D(P_s,P_{\psi_i})=\sqrt{1-(1-2/N)^2}=2\sqrt{N-1}/N=O(N^{-1/2})$. This tends to zero with $N$.

Suppose instead the mark is unknown and uniform on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Each $P_{\psi_i}$ is a density operator by [F4], so their finite average $\rho=N^{-1}\sum_iP_{\psi_i}$ is self-adjoint, nonnegative, and trace one. Writing $e_i=|i-1\rangle$, expansion gives $P_{\psi_i}=P_s-\frac2{\sqrt N}(|s\rangle\langle e_i|+|e_i\rangle\langle s|)+\frac4N|e_i\rangle\langle e_i|$. The two cross sums each equal $\sqrt N P_s$, and $\sum_i|e_i\rangle\langle e_i|=I$ by [F2]–[F3], so $\rho=(1-4/N)P_s+4I/N^2$. Then $X=\rho-P_s$ has eigenvalue $-4(N-1)/N^2$ on $\operatorname{span}\{s\}$ and $4/N^2$ on $s^\perp$ of dimension $N-1$; their sum with multiplicity is zero, so $X$ is trace-zero. Its negative part is $X_-=(4(N-1)/N^2)P_s$, whose trace is $4(N-1)/N^2$ because $P_s$ has trace one. By [F5] and [F7], $D(\rho,P_s)=\tfrac12\|X\|_1=4(N-1)/N^2=O(N^{-1})$. If $N=1$, $s^\perp$ has dimension zero and the formula gives distance zero.

Fix an address-valued final measurement, let $r_i$ be its probability of output $i$ on $P_s$, and let $p_i(i)$ be its probability of outputting $i$ on $P_{\psi_i}$. The event form of [F8] and step 1.1 give $p_i(i)\le r_i+2\sqrt{N-1}/N$. Since $\sum_i r_i\le1$, the average success for a uniformly unknown marked coordinate is at most $N^{-1}+2\sqrt{N-1}/N$, which tends to zero. Separately, [F8] and step 1.2 bound the total-variation change between the empty-input law and the uniform-mark mixture law by $4(N-1)/N^2$, so this specified experiment also has vanishing decision advantage. The lower bound [F9] concerns arbitrary algorithms and is proved independently; it is not inferred from this example.
